summary: Describes the Simple Nomenclator Query Protocol, which lets a client talk to a descriptive name service or similar relational-style query service. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: It is the language a program uses to ask a name directory a question and get back matching entries.

questions: how to query a nomenclator server
how does snqp handle distributed queries
what is a t-bound in snqp
subtitle: A protocol for querying descriptive name services and other relational databases.

tldr.problem: Users need a way to query distributed name and information services that may store data in different formats or protocols. A standard protocol would let clients search multiple data repositories without knowing their implementation details.
tldr.mechanism: SNQP is a simple text-based query protocol that accepts SQL queries from clients, translates them for different backend data repositories, and returns integrated results. It runs over TCP and uses reply codes similar to SMTP.
tldr.outcome: Clients can query distributed information services using standard SQL, with support for caching information freshness, query cost advice, and graphical user interface integration. The protocol has remained informational but has seen use beyond the original Nomenclator system.

facts.value: Default (exact match with wildcards) and CCSO (word-based)

today: RFC 2259 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It remains the definition of the Simple Nomenclator Query Protocol, though it has seen limited adoption outside the Nomenclator system for which it was designed.

sections.title: What SNQP Does
sections.content:
SNQP (Simple Nomenclator Query Protocol) lets programs ask questions of distributed name and information services. A user describes what information they want using standard SQL queries, and SNQP servers translate these queries to work with whatever data repositories are behind them, whether those repositories are relational databases, CCSO name servers, X.500 directories, or something else entirely.

SNQP was designed for the Nomenclator service, which integrates information from many different sources. But it also works as a query language for single repositories. The server handles the complexity of talking to different backend systems, so clients see one unified interface.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask SNQP a question in a simple format, and it figures out how to get the answer from whatever sources are available, even if those sources don't normally understand each other.

sections.title: How the Protocol Works
sections.content:
SNQP is a connection-oriented protocol using TCP. A client connects to a well-known port on an SNQP server and then issues commands. The server responds with reply codes that tell the client whether each command succeeded, plus the data it requested.

The client starts by discovering what relations (tables) are available and what attributes (columns) they have. Then the client submits SQL queries in a block, and the server returns results as they arrive from the various data repositories it contacts. The protocol supports multiple queries in one block, which the client can stop or skip if needed.

SNQP also supports different comparison operators: exact string matching (the default) or CCSO-style word matching, so it works with different kinds of backends. For graphical user interface clients, the server can provide detailed error messages with line and column numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: You connect, ask what questions are allowed, then ask your question in SQL. The server says yes or no, and if yes, it sends back matching results.

sections.title: Queries, Caching, and Freshness
sections.content:
When a client submits an SQL query, the SNQP server may contact one or many data repositories. If some are unavailable, the server can return partial results and tell the client which repositories failed, so the query can be resubmitted to just those sources later.

SNQP servers often cache data to speed up queries. The protocol includes a t-bound (time-bound), which indicates the age of the oldest piece of cached data used in the response. A client can request fresher information by specifying a more recent t-bound, which tells the server to bypass or refresh older cache entries.

Clients can also ask for advice before executing a query: what repositories will be contacted, which attributes might constrain the search, and what values are possible for an attribute. This lets users understand the cost of their query before running it.
sections.plainLanguage: SNQP tells you when its answer might be old, lets you ask for fresher information, and can warn you before a big search that might take a long time.

sections.title: Commands and Replies
sections.content:
SNQP defines about a dozen commands. Key commands include relations (list available tables), attributes (list columns in a table), query (submit SQL queries), advice (show cost estimates without running the query), and compare (choose the style of string matching).

Other commands help with protocol control: next stops the current query and starts the next one in a block, stop cancels all remaining queries, and quit ends the session. Graphical user interface clients can send imagui to get more detailed error reports, with line and column numbers for SQL syntax errors.

Server replies use three-digit codes like SMTP. Codes in the 200s mean success, 300s mean the operation is in progress, 400s mean temporary problems, and 500s mean permanent errors. For GUI clients, special codes provide formatted error reports with exact error locations.
sections.plainLanguage: You send commands like "show me the tables" or "run this question," and the server answers with a number code that tells you if it worked or what went wrong.

sections.title: Security Limits
sections.content:
RFC 2259 notes that SNQP servers and clients depend on the Domain Name Service to locate each other, so they inherit DNS security issues. The protocol itself does not include any procedures for protecting the information sent to or from an SNQP server.

SNQP was designed for trusted environments where the network path between client and server is secure, or where the data is not sensitive. If confidentiality or integrity of data in transit is required, encryption would need to be added separately, or SNQP would need to be used over a secure channel.
sections.plainLanguage: SNQP assumes you trust the people on your network and doesn't have built-in ways to keep answers secret or prove they came from a real server.
